raw_response_text: {"task_id":"RT07","claim_assessments":[{"claim_text":"PFAS are transferred from bulk water into a PFAS‑rich foam or foamate, often with substantial enrichment and volume reduction, while treated water retains reduced but non‑zero PFAS levels [S01; S07; S09; S11; S13; S15; S16].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S07","S09","S11","S13","S15","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"All cited studies describe foam fractionation as transferring PFAS from bulk water/leachate into foam/foamate, with reduced but non-zero PFAS remaining in treated water: S01 (landfill leachate, ~60% ΣPFAS removal, foamate ~10% volume), S07 (municipal wastewater; PFAS removed to foamate, FFout still contains PFAS), S09 (NF concentrate FF; permeate cleaned, retentate and foamate streams with PFAS), S11 (landfill leachate; PFAS concentrated in foamate up to 800 µg/L, bulk residuals), S13 & S15 (SAFF groundwater/leachate where treated water still has ng/L PFAS, and foamate is enriched), S16 (effluent and leachate cases with enriched foam and residual PFAS in bottom solution). All support phase transfer with enrichment and non-zero residuals."},{"claim_text":"Multiple studies explicitly position foam fractionation as the first step in a treatment train that must be followed by destruction or polishing adsorption processes [S01; S07; S08; S09; S11; S12; S13; S14; S16].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S07","S08","S09","S11","S12","S13","S14","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S01-E01 & E05 describe FF as a suitable first step in a treatment train and propose downstream degradative treatment of concentrated foam by plasma or EO. S07-E06 & E08 note FF foamate should undergo further fractionation and final destruction and mention integration with other WWTP processes. S08-E01 & E04 frame FF explicitly as a preconcentration step before EO. S09-E07 & E08 propose downstream destruction (EO, incineration) for foamate and AIX polishing for FF retentate. S11-E04 mentions ozone FF followed by destruction technologies (plasma, thermal, EO). S12-E02–E04 model FF plus incineration and discuss FF as separation front-end, comparing to GAC/IX and hybrid trains. S13-E03 discusses SAFF as separation+concentration followed by incineration or development of destruction cells. S14-E01 & E04 explicitly focus on coupling FF with HALT as a concentration–destruction train. S16-E02, E04, E06 emphasize FF as a separation step that leaves residual PFAS and produces a concentrated foam suitable for disposal or further treatment. Collectively they position FF as an initial concentration step, not a stand‑alone solution."},{"claim_text":"In synthetic groundwater without co‑surfactant, long‑chain PFOS and PFOA achieved plateau removals of ~90% and ~60%, respectively, at ~40 µg/L [S10].","cited_source_ids":["S10"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S10-E06 describes a control experiment in synthetic groundwater with no co‑surfactant where initial concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, PFBS, PFBA were ~40 µg/L and states that long‑chain PFOS and PFOA exhibited rapid removal, plateauing at approximately 90% and 60% respectively. This matches the claim."},{"claim_text":"Short‑chain PFBS and PFBA performed worse than PFOS and PFOA in the same synthetic groundwater control, consistent with lower surface activity [S10].","cited_source_ids":["S10"],"status":"partially_supported","rationale":"S10-E06 states PFOS and PFOA plateau at ~90% and ~60% removal and that PFBS and PFBA were part of the experiment with no co-surfactant and lower surface excess; however the excerpt truncates after mentioning PFBS and PFBA, without explicitly giving their plateau removals. The record-level assessment notes that PFBS/PFBA had lower performance, but the provided chunk doesn’t quantify this. The qualitative statement that they ‘performed worse’ is consistent with lower surface activity but only implicitly supported here."},{"claim_text":"Adding CTAB as a cationic co‑surfactant in synthetic groundwater expanded performance across 0.4–400 µg/L and achieved near‑complete removal of PFOS and PFOA in ~5 min, while PFBS and PFBA required ~50 min at the highest concentration to reach high removals, with 99% removal reported for PFBS and PFBA at the highest concentration [S10].","cited_source_ids":["S10"],"status":"partially_supported","rationale":"S10-E02 and E05 (co‑surfactant tests) state that each PFAS was tested individually over 400–400,000 ng/L and that PFOS and PFOA exhibited near-complete removal in as short as 5 minutes. They also state that for PFBS and PFBA at the highest initial concentration (400,000 ng/L), 99% removal was achieved and that ‘the same level of removal was achieved for PFBS and PFBA after approximately 50 minutes of operation.’ However, the explicit link between the 99% value and the ‘~50 minutes’ time is partly inferred across sentences. The concentration range (0.4–400 µg/L) and near‑complete long‑chain removal in ~5 min are supported; the precise co‑occurrence of 99% and 50 min for the short‑chains is only indirectly stated, so the claim is slightly more specific than the excerpt."},{"claim_text":"In real Australian groundwater with SDS as co‑foaming agent, bench‑scale foam fractionation reduced PFHxS, PFOA and PFOS to below 0.1 ppb (detection limit) within 60 min, whereas PFBA was not effectively removed [S03].","cited_source_ids":["S03"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S03-E06 states that foam fractionation with SDS removed PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS from Australian groundwater to below the analytical detection limit of 0.1 ppb within 60 min, but was unable to remove short-chain PFBA. S07-E02 states that in all sludge experiments, formed foamate had higher TS content than the bulk liquor, visually apparent and confirmed by TS. While PFAS co-concentration with solids is logically implied by foam fractionation, the excerpt does not explicitly state PFAS enrichment in the solids-laden foamate; that part is interpretive. Thus lower PFAS removal and higher solids in foamate are supported; explicit PFAS co-concentration with biomass is inferred."},{"claim_text":"Across matrices and scales, short‑chain PFAS removal is consistently weaker than that for long‑chain PFAS in simple air‑only foam fractionation [S01; S03; S07; S08; S09; S11; S12; S15; S16].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S03","S07","S08","S09","S11","S12","S15","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"Multiple sources report systematically lower removal for short-chain PFAS: S01-E03 (certain short-chains <30% vs >90% long-chains), S03-E02/E06 (PFBA poorly removed while PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS removed well), S07-E07 (long-chains have higher affinity for foam and sludge than short-chains, with minimal PFDA removal), S08-E06 (FF more effective for long-chains), S09-E05/E07 (short-chain-enriched retentate after FF; co-surfactants needed to boost short-chain removal), S11-E03 (short-chains 8–95% vs long-chains >90%, with some ultra‑short <10% recovery), S12-E02/E05 (LCA text notes long-chain removal >90% and short-chain typically ≤50%), S15-E03/E06 (short-chains poorly removed by SAFF, dominating residuals), S16-E01/E02/E04 (short-chains show lower removal and high residuals). S10-E02/E05 show that CTAB-enhanced FF achieved 99% removal for PFBS and PFBA at the highest concentration and improved short‑chain removal kinetics compared to controls. S07-E03 shows K15(+) increased PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA removals substantially. These data support marked improvements for the specified short-chains."},{"claim_text":"In synthetic systems using OTCS with micro‑nano bubbles, PFOA and PFOS removals approached ~99% in synthetic water; in natural lake and reservoir waters PFOA/PFOS removals exceeded 80% [S04].","cited_source_ids":["S04"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S04-E07/E05 report that the OTCS-MNBs system achieved removal efficiencies of 98.73% and 99.21% for PFOA and PFOS in synthetic water. This aligns with the claim."},{"claim_text":"Foam fractionation energy demand is qualitatively characterized as low‑energy and low‑consumables compared to membrane and EO systems [S01-E01; S08-E04; S16-E05].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S08","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S01-E01 notes that FF is suitable for dilute solutions using only air, eliminating chemicals, solvents, filter materials and adsorbents, implying low consumables. This supports the claim."},{"claim_text":"In the LCA scenarios, foam wastes are assumed to go to hazardous waste incineration as the base‑case end‑of‑life option [S12].","cited_source_ids":["S12"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S12-E03 describes that in the one-stage systems, extracted foam (1% or 20% of input volume) is sent to hazardous waste incineration as the disposal unit. Thus the claim is supported."},{"claim_text":"At AACO, SAFF tertiary foamate is stored on‑site and the default disposal pathway is high‑temperature incineration, pending development of on‑site destruction cells [S13].","cited_source_ids":["S13"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S13-E01/E03 describe that tertiary foamate, highly enriched in PFAS with reduced volume, is stored on-site awaiting periodic disposal, and S13-E03 states that default disposal of the highly enriched PFAS waste is high‑temperature incineration, with preference for future on-site destruction cells under development. This matches the claim."},{"claim_text":"In the pilot FF+EO study, overall mean PFAS degradation across treatment trains was ~50%, with long‑chains degraded up to 86% and short‑chains up to 31% [S08].","cited_source_ids":["S08"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S08-E05 states that the mean total PFAS degradation over the designed treatment train reached 50%, with long- and short-chain PFAS degrading up to 86% and 31%, respectively. This exactly matches."},{"claim_text":"Stirred‑batch foam fractionation removed 80–90% of 14C‑PFOA from synthetic solutions in 30 min, and 90–100% of PFOA in foamate was mineralized to 14CO₂ during electrochemical oxidation [S06].","cited_source_ids":["S06"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S06-E06 reports that foam fractionation can remove 80–90% of PFOA in 200 mL stirred-batch tests within 30 min and that 90–100% of PFOA in the concentrated foamate was oxidized via EO, converting -14COOH to 14CO₂. This matches the claim."},{"claim_text":"In landfill leachate, single‑stage foam fractionation transferred ~80% of TOC into foam while PFAS contributed <0.01% of TOC; PFAS precursors were concentrated in foamate, as indicated by TOP assay increases in PFCAs and PFOS after oxidative assay [S16].","cited_source_ids":["S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S16-E06 states that ~80% of TOC ended up in foam solution, PFAS accounted for <0.01% of TOC, and that TOP assay after FF showed increased PFCAs (PFBA, PFPeA, PFHpA, PFOA) and PFOS in original, treated, and foam samples, consistent with precursor transformation during TOP. This supports the claim that precursors are concentrated in foamate and revealed by TOP."},{"claim_text":"Across landfill leachate and municipal wastewater, foam‑based concentration is robust for long‑chain PFAS, can be enhanced for some short‑chains with co‑surfactants, ozonation, or low‑pH operation, but still tends to leave residual short‑chain PFAS in treated water [S01; S02; S03; S05; S07; S09; S11; S15; S16].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S02","S03","S05","S07","S09","S11","S15","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"S01 (pilot leachate) shows >90% long-chain removal, poor short-chain removal. S02 (leachate with cosurfactants) shows 1.2–4 log long-chain, 1–2 log short-chain for some species. S03 groundwater experiments show PFBA (short-chain) not removed even with SDS. S05 (MER and pH 2 foaming) demonstrates high long-chain and improved, but not complete, short-chain capture, with residual short-chain PFCAs. S11 highlights >90% long-chain removal in leachate, short-chains 8–95% with incomplete removal. S15 shows SAFF leaves a residual load dominated by short-chains. S16 across matrices notes better removal for long-chains, short-chains consistently poorer and residuals at 10²–10³ ng/L in leachate. Collectively, this supports the summarized pattern."},{"claim_text":"Foam fractionation by itself does not destroy PFAS and often leaves short‑chain PFAS and precursors at levels incompatible with the lowest health‑based criteria; it produces foamate that is co‑contaminated with organics and sometimes solids, requiring downstream management [S01; S03; S05; S07; S08; S11; S13; S14; S16].","cited_source_ids":["S01","S03","S05","S07","S08","S11","S13","S14","S16"],"status":"supported","rationale":"Multiple studies explicitly state FF is a separation/concentration method, not a degradation one: S01-E01/E05, S08-E01/E04, S13-E08, S16-E05. Review task:
{"review_brief":"Prepare a focused review of when foam fractionation is useful as a concentration step and how the resulting PFAS-rich foamate should be managed.","task_id":"RT07","title":"Placing foam fractionation within a PFAS treatment train"}

Candidate review:
## 1. Role of Foam Fractionation as a Concentration Step

Across the evidence base, foam fractionation (FF) is consistently used and evaluated as a **phase‑transfer/concentration technology**, not as a destructive process:

- PFAS are transferred from bulk water into a PFAS‑rich foam or foamate, often with substantial enrichment and volume reduction, while treated water retains reduced but non‑zero PFAS levels [S01; S07; S09; S11; S13; S15; S16].
- Multiple studies explicitly position FF as the **first step in a treatment train** that must be followed by destruction (e.g., electrochemical oxidation, plasma, HALT, incineration) or by polishing adsorption processes [S01; S07; S08; S09; S11; S12; S13; S14; S16].

Any assessment of “treatment success” must therefore include both:  
(1) performance of the FF step as a concentrator, and  
(2) disposition or destruction of the PFAS‑rich foamate or secondary concentrates.

---

## 2. Performance Across Scales and Matrices

### 2.1 Groundwater and Drinking‑Water Contexts

**Bench‑scale synthetic and real groundwater**

- In synthetic groundwater without co‑surfactant, long‑chain PFOS and PFOA achieved plateau removals of ~90% and ~60%, respectively, at ~40 µg/L [S10]. Short‑chain PFBS and PFBA performed worse, consistent with lower surface activity [S10].
- Adding CTAB as a cationic co‑surfactant in synthetic groundwater expanded performance across a wide concentration range (0.4–400 µg/L). Long‑chain PFOS and PFOA achieved near‑complete removal in ~5 min, whereas PFBS and PFBA required ~50 min at the highest concentration to reach high removals, with 99% removal reported for both short‑chain PFBS and PFBA at the highest test concentration [S10].
- In real Australian groundwater with SDS as co‑foaming agent, bench‑scale FF reduced PFHxS, PFOA and PFOS to below 0.1 ppb (detection limit) within 60 min, whereas PFBA was not effectively removed [S03]. This underscores strong chain‑length selectivity in realistic matrices.

**Pilot‑scale foam fractionation on groundwater**

- A pilot groundwater FF + EO train achieved **~60% mean ΣPFAS removal in the FF step**, with ~90% removal of long‑chain PFAA and weaker removal of short‑chain PFAS [S08].
- A commercial SAFF deployment on PFAS‑contaminated groundwater (AACO) previously achieved ≥99.8% removal of PFOS and PFOA and ≥98.4% of PFHxS, with post‑SAFF concentrations ≤12, ≤1 and ≤17 ng/L, respectively [S13-E06]. Those data are for groundwater, but detailed foamate volumes and energy use are not given for that trial [S13].

**Nanofiltration–FF treatment trains for drinking water**

- A pilot NF plant treating AFFF‑impacted municipal groundwater reduced total detectable PFAS in permeate from ~77 ng/L to 1.4 ng/L; ΣPFAS4 from 56 ng/L to 1.0 ng/L [S09].
- Continuous pilot FF of the NF concentrate removed ~90±1% of total PFAS using air alone and 94% with a cationic co‑surfactant [S09].
- The combined NF+FF train shifted PFAS into:
  - A small foamate stream (~2% of NF feed volume) at >3000 ng/L (41× feed concentration) [S09], and
  - A retentate (~18% of NF feed volume) enriched in short‑chain PFAS, at 35 ng/L without co‑surfactant and 21 ng/L with co‑surfactant [S09].

This shows FF is effective as a **post‑NF concentrator**, particularly for long‑chain PFAS, while leaving a shorter‑chain‑enriched retentate that may require ion exchange polishing [S09].

### 2.2 Landfill Leachate

**Pilot‑scale continuous FF on raw leachate**

- A pilot continuous FF column treating real landfill leachate achieved **~60% plateau ΣPFAS removal**, with >90% removal for individual long‑chain PFAS and <30% removal for certain short‑chain PFAS [S01].
- Foamate volume was reduced to ~10% of inlet volume [S01].
- Mass balance was imperfect, with visual evidence of aerosols and possible matrix‑driven transformations [S01].

**Bench‑scale FF and hybrid MER systems on leachate**

- Bench‑scale FF with co‑surfactants in leachate achieved 1.2–4 log reductions for long‑chain PFAS and 1–2 logs for some short‑chain compounds when cationic/zwitterionic cosurfactants were used [S02].
- Bench‑scale landfill leachate FF at low ng/L–µg/L levels across multiple matrices showed >70% removal for most monitored PFAS, but systematically lower removal for short‑chains [S16].

**Membrane electrochemical reactor (MER) with foam fractionation**

- A low‑pH (~2) MER treating leachate achieved 95.6% total PFAS removal, with 98.3% removal of PFSAs and 85.5% of PFCAs [S05]. Short‑chain PFSAs (C≤6) reached 92.5–99.1% removal; short‑chain PFCAs (C≤6) 80.8–90% [S05].
- Residual short‑chain PFCAs in defoamed leachate remained non‑trivial (e.g., 19.2% of PFBA mass, 15.6% PFPeA, 10% PFHxA) [S05].
- Volume of defoamed leachate after MER was only 24% of the initial volume, with the remainder entrained in foam and solids [S05].

This MER configuration is not pure FF, but it shows that combining foam‑based separation with in‑situ electrochemical processes can greatly improve short‑chain capture compared to foam‑only treatments.

**Ozone vs air foam fractionation on leachate**

- Bench‑scale ozone FF removed >90% long‑chain PFAS and 8–95% of named short‑chains; some ultrashort species (<4 perfluorinated carbons) had recoveries <10% [S11].
- Long‑chain PFAS in bulk leachate dropped below 0.03–0.05 µg/L within 2–6 min; complete short‑chain removal was not achievable in that timeframe [S11].
- Ozone FF produced **foamate volumes 2–4× lower** than air FF and foamate wettability <4% vs 7–13% for air, while still concentrating PFAS up to 800 µg/L and increasing the number of detected PFAS (including several precursors) in foamate [S11].
- Air FF in the same leachate saw 10–30 percentage‑point gains in removal for short‑chains (PFHxA, PFPeS) and ~20 points for PFOA when increasing air flow from 0.5 to 1 L/min, but remained less effective for the very short‑chains [S11].

**Simple pH‑induced foaming**

- Acidification of leachate to pH 2.0 without electrochemistry separated 83.1% of total PFAS into foam and 11.3% into precipitated solids; with 0.1 M NaHCO₃ pre‑addition, foam‑phase separation increased to 92.5% [S05].
- Short‑chains (C≤6) were still partitioned significantly into foam (59.2–84.7%) and solids (5.7–13%) [S05].

Collectively, these leachate studies show that **foam‑based concentration is robust for long‑chains**, can be enhanced for some short‑chains with co‑surfactants, ozonation, or low‑pH operation, but still tends to leave residual short‑chain PFAS in treated leachate.

### 2.3 Municipal Wastewater and WWTP Effluent

**Biologically treated municipal wastewater (no or limited surfactant)**

- Batch FF on several MBR/MBBR/CAS effluents achieved average removals of:
  - 96±1% for ΣPFAS4,
  - 93±1% for ΣPFOAeq,
  - 53±2% for ΣPFAS21 [S07].
- Biologically treated effluents had low foaming potential; foam (top water layer) was removed by suction rather than a stable overflowing foam [S07].
- A fixed foamate extraction of 8% of treated liquid volume was used; authors judged it difficult to reduce this below ~5% without loss of performance, based on earlier studies [S07].

**Effect of cationic surfactant on short‑chain PFAS**

- Adding cationic surfactant K15(+) in MBR effluents raised removal of:
  - PFHpA from 48% to >76% (MBRsed),
  - PFPeA from 16% to 44% (MBRout),
  - PFHxA from 29% to >89% (MBRout; statistically significant) [S07].

**Sludge‑integrated operation**

- FF applied directly to sludge liquors (MBRsludge, CASsludge) showed **significantly lower PFAS removal** than for corresponding treated effluents [S07].
- Foamate from sludge matrices had higher total solids than the bulk liquid, so FF co‑concentrated biomass/solids with PFAS [S07].

These results suggest FF can be used as a **side‑stream or post‑biological concentrator**, but foaming and co‑concentration of solids complicate integration with biological treatment, especially if surfactants are added.

**WWTP effluent at low ng/L**

- A multi‑stage FF with added thickener (HPMC) treated WWTP effluent with initial PFOS and PFOA of 34.8 and 8.6 ng/L. After treatment, both were <5 ng/L, corresponding to 99% and 94% removal, respectively [S16].
- PFOS and PFOA were enriched 19× and 17× in third‑stage foam relative to the original effluent; mass recovery for most PFAS (except PFBA) was 70–130% [S16].

At very low ng/L levels, FF can still provide meaningful concentration and removal for long‑chains when assisted by thickeners.

### 2.4 Landfill Leachate and WWTP Combined View

- In landfill leachate, single‑stage FF left PFBA, PFOA and PFOS in the bottom solution at 10²–10³ ng/L after first stage, despite high nominal removals, indicating that FF alone cannot achieve the very low health advisory levels and must be paired with GAC/IX or other polishing [S16].
- FF co‑concentrated ~80% of TOC into foam, while PFAS were <0.01% of TOC, highlighting that **organic co‑contaminants dominate foamate mass** [S16].

---

## 3. Short‑Chain PFAS Recovery

Across matrices and scales, **short‑chain PFAS removal is consistently weaker** than that for long‑chain PFAS, but there are clear variations:

- **Poor short‑chain performance in air‑only FF**  
  - Pilot continuous FF on leachate: <30% removal for certain short‑chains vs >90% for long‑chains [S01].
  - Commercial SAFF on landfill leachate: post‑SAFF sum of SLV‑11 PFAS was 1260 ng/L, dominated by short‑chain PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeA, PFBA, while longer‑chains summed to only 14.4 ng/L [S15].
  - Bench‑scale synthetic groundwater controls: PFBS and PFBA had much lower plateaus than PFOS/PFOA [S10].
  - Bench‑scale groundwater FF with SDS: PFBA remained largely unremoved [S03].

- **Enhanced short‑chain capture via co‑surfactants and process intensification**
  - Cationic co‑surfactants (CTAB, Montaline C40, K15(+)) markedly improved PFPeA, PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeS removal in synthetic and NF‑concentrate systems [S09, S10, S07].
  - MER operation at low pH with foam fractionation achieved 80.8–90% removal of short‑chain PFCAs and 92.5–99.1% for short‑chain PFSAs [S05].
  - Simple pH‑induced foaming plus solids formation at pH 2 captured 59.2–84.7% of short‑chains into foam and 5.7–13% into solids [S05].
  - In synthetic systems using OTCS with micro‑nano bubbles, PFOA and PFOS removals approached ~99% in synthetic water [S04]; in natural lake and reservoir waters PFOA/PFOS removals exceeded 80% [S04]. These are long‑chains, but improved foam stability and interfacial area could, in principle, benefit some shorter chains.

- **Precursors and transformation**  
  FF often concentrates precursors into foam; TOP‑assay evidence in landfill leachate showed increased PFCAs and PFOS after oxidative assay, consistent with precursor presence in foam and treated leachate [S16]. Ozone FF concentrated several precursors (6:2 FTCA, PFECHS, FOSA, 8:2 FTS, N‑MeFOSAA) into foamate [S11].

In summary, **short‑chain PFAS are not reliably removed by simple air FF** at environmentally relevant concentrations. Co‑surfactants, low‑pH operation, hybrid electrochemical systems, or multi‑stage designs can partially overcome this limitation but rarely to the degree achieved for long‑chains.

---

## 4. Volume Reduction, Enrichment Factors, and Foamate Characteristics

### 4.1 Volume Reduction and Foamate Fractions

Quantified volume reductions span several orders of magnitude depending on configuration:

- **Direct leachate or wastewater FF (single‑step)**  
  - Pilot leachate FF: foamate volume ~10% of inlet [S01].  
  - Municipal wastewater FF: foamate extraction 8% of treated volume [S07].

- **NF–FF trains for drinking water**  
  - NF concentrate FF: foamate ~2% of NF feed volume; FF retentate ~18% [S09].

- **Ozone vs air FF**  
  - Ozone FF: foamate volumes 2–4× lower than air FF for the same leachate matrix, with wettability <4% vs 7–13% for air FF [S11].

- **Modelled multi‑stage FF for groundwater**  
  - Conceptual multi‑stage FF treating 1,000,000 m³ of groundwater was modelled to yield:
    - 154 m³ concentrate for a 2‑stage process, and
    - 0.6 m³ concentrate for a 3‑stage FF [S14].

- **Life‑cycle FF configurations (landfill leachate)**  
  - One‑stage FF with 20% foam fraction: 200 m³ foam waste per 1000 m³ leachate treated [S12].
  - One‑stage FF with 1% foam fraction: 10 m³ foam waste per 1000 m³ (by inference from foam fraction), though only the fraction itself (1%) is explicitly quantified [S12].
  - Three‑stage low‑foam FF: very low foam waste volumes are reported conceptually; residual foam waste per 1000 m³ is stated as <0.0006 m³ under some configurations [S12-E04], though specific to that scenario.

These values show that depending on design, foamate volume can range from **1–20% of influent** at unit scale to **sub‑percent levels via multistage concentration** or NF–FF combinations.

### 4.2 Enrichment Factors and Concentrations

Where enrichment is quantified:

- NF concentrate FF (drinking water): 41× enrichment in foamate relative to NF feed; foamate >3000 ng/L [S09].
- WWTP effluent FF with HPMC: PFOS and PFOA enriched 19× and 17× in third‑stage foam vs original effluent [S16].
- Mixed environmental waters: PFAS in final foams “up to over 30×” initial concentrations [S16].
- Ozone FF on leachate: total PFAS in foamate up to 800 µg/L, with a broader PFAS/precursor spectrum than in original leachate [S11].
- Leachate TOC co‑concentration: ~80% of TOC partitioned to foam in single‑stage FF, while PFAS represented <0.01% of TOC [S16].

### 4.3 Foamate Wetness and Co‑contaminants

- Air FF foamate is typically **wetter and more voluminous** (7–13% wettability; 2–4× ozone foamate volume) [S11].
- Foamate from sludge or mixed liquor is enriched in total solids and biomass [S07].
- Foamate from leachates and membrane concentrates contains high TOC and diverse co‑surfactants [S09, S16].

Thus, **foamate is not a “pure PFAS” stream**; it is a concentrated mixed waste that can be dominated volumetrically and chemically by non‑PFAS organics and, in some cases, solids.

---

## 5. Operational Stability and Energy Demand

### 5.1 Operational Stability

Evidence on long‑term continuous operation is limited:

- The NF pilot ran for almost 6 months, but FF was evaluated in shorter campaigns [S09].
- SAFF groundwater trials at AACO ran over years; for landfill leachate, only limited data are reported in the provided excerpts [S13, S15].
- Bench‑scale studies typically ran for minutes to an hour; few report extended continuous FF operation.

Foaming behavior is matrix‑dependent:

- Biologically treated wastewater had low foaming potential, requiring suction of the top water layer [S07].
- Sludge‑containing matrices produced foamate rich in solids, potentially problematic for hydraulics and downstream handling [S07].
- High ionic strength and added surfactants generally improved foam stability and PFAS removal [S01-E07, S03-E07, S09, S10-E05, S16-E07], but also increase co‑transfer of non‑PFAS organics.

### 5.2 Energy Demand

Direct measured FF energy use is sparse; we rely on:

- Qualitative characterizations: FF is described as **low energy, low consumables**, particularly compared to membrane and EO systems [S01-E01; S08-E04; S16-E05].
- Conceptual modelling:  
  - For multi‑stage FF treating 1,000,000 m³ groundwater, total FF energy was assumed to be ~0.8 kWh/m³, i.e., 800,000 kWh [S14].
  - HALT treatment of the resulting concentrates added only 2.5–6.7% more energy in the 2‑stage scenario and <0.03% in the 3‑stage scenario [S14].
- Life‑cycle GWP surrogates (landfill leachate FF):
  - One‑stage 20% foam fraction: 818 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ [S12].
  - One‑stage 1% foam fraction: 357 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ [S12].
  - Three‑stage FF: 402 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ [S12].

These LCA values integrate compressed‑air energy and foam waste incineration burdens; they confirm that **lower foam fractions and multistage concentration can materially reduce life‑cycle climate impacts** while producing a much smaller hazardous waste volume.

Energy data for hybrid FF+EO systems are not quantitatively given, but qualitative statements indicate that treating all water directly with EO is markedly more energy‑intensive than treating only concentrated foam, due to ~10‑fold larger treated volume [S08-E03].

---

## 6. Management and Downstream Treatment of PFAS‑Rich Foamate

Foamate management is central to any FF‑based treatment train.

### 6.1 Direct Disposal with Incineration

- The SAFF tertiary foamate at AACO is stored on‑site and the default disposal pathway is **high‑temperature incineration**, pending development of on‑site destruction cells [S13].
- LCA scenarios for landfill leachate FF assume **hazardous waste incineration** for foam wastes as the base‑case end‑of‑life option [S12].
- These LCAs highlight:
  - A one‑stage 20% foam fraction produces 200 m³ foam waste per 1000 m³ leachate treated and has the highest GWP [S12].
  - A 1% one‑stage and multistage low‑foam configurations substantially reduce foam waste volume and GWP [S12, S12-E04].

Thus, **overly large foamate fractions (e.g., 20%) can dominate life‑cycle environmental footprint via incineration burdens**, even if PFAS removal is good.

### 6.2 Electrochemical Oxidation (EO) of Foamate

Multiple studies evaluate EO as a destruction step for PFAS‑rich concentrates:

- **Pilot FF + EO (groundwater, leachate)**  
  - Overall mean PFAS degradation across FF+EO treatment trains was ~50%, with long‑chains degraded up to 86% and short‑chains up to 31% [S08].
  - EO of leachate‑derived foam improved toxicity metrics dramatically (TTR binding reductions up to 89%; bacterial toxicity up to 94% in some cases), but PFSA degradation in foam was limited, leaving persistent sulfonates [S08].
  - Authors explicitly recommend verifying at full scale that all PFAS removed in FF end up in foam and are degraded in EO, and note low PFSA degradation as a key limitation [S08].

- **Radiolabeled 14C‑PFOA systems (synthetic and natural waters)**  
  - Stirred‑batch FF removed 80–90% of 14C‑PFOA from synthetic solutions in 30 min, with 90–100% of PFOA in the foamate mineralized to ¹⁴CO₂ during EO [S06].
  - In 3500 mL double‑tank tests, FF removed 90% of PFOA from WWTP effluent but only 50% from drainage‑ditch water; EO half‑lives for PFOA in foamate were 8.7–15 min for both matrices, again with mineralization of the PFOA carbon to ¹⁴CO₂ [S06].

EO is clearly effective for some PFAS in foamate (notably PFOA), but **sulfonates and complex mixtures remain problematic**, and energy demand is non‑negligible, though reduced by concentrating PFAS first.

### 6.3 Hydrothermal Alkaline Treatment (HALT) of Foam Concentrates

- Two foam concentrates from FF field demonstrations (FC1 primary foam and FC2 tertiary foam) with initial PFAS up to g/L levels were treated by HALT at 350 °C, 1 M NaOH [S14].
- Results:
  - >90% **degradation and defluorination** of all 62 identified PFAS (anions, cations, zwitterions) within 90 min [S14].
  - Inorganic fluoride production was consistent with essentially complete C–F bond cleavage [S14].
- Residuals:
  - Even after a hypothetical 99% PFAS mass removal, residual PFAS concentrations in the small treated concentrate volume are expected to be mg/L–µg/L, still orders of magnitude above original groundwater; blending treated concentrate back into the large FF influent stream is proposed instead of direct discharge [S14].
  - HALT‑recalcitrant dissolved organic matter and NaOH are likewise proposed to be managed via dilution in the large influent stream [S14].

Conceptual energy analysis suggests HALT adds only a few percent to the FF energy footprint if applied to small concentrate volumes [S14]. HALT is therefore a compelling **second‑stage destruction option for highly concentrated foamates**.

### 6.4 Other Proposed Downstream Options

- **Plasma and electrochemical oxidation** are repeatedly proposed for treating concentrated foamates from FF of leachate and groundwater; prior studies cited in S01 show both effective PFAS removal, with plasma avoiding short‑chain byproducts observed under EO [S01].
- **Evaporation plus incineration of residual solids** is proposed for NF‑concentrate foamates [S09].
- **Polishing adsorption (anion exchange resins)** is recommended for short‑chain‑enriched FF retentates (not foamate) in drinking‑water applications [S09].

### 6.5 Treatment Train Design Considerations

The evidence supports FF as an advantageous concentration step when:

- **Influent PFAS concentrations are modest to high** (leachate, NF concentrates, AFFF‑impacted groundwater), allowing reasonable PFAS mass recovery in foam, and
- **Downstream destructive capacity is constrained**: by concentrating PFAS into <1–10% of the original volume, energy‑intensive technologies (EO, HALT, plasma) or costly incineration can be applied to a much smaller mass of water, improving feasibility [S01, S08, S09, S11, S12, S14, S16].

However, **FF alone does not yield regulatory‑compliant discharges in challenging matrices** (e.g., landfill leachate), particularly due to short‑chains and precursors [S15, S16].

---

## 7. When Is Foam Fractionation “Useful” as a Concentration Step?

Synthesizing across lab, pilot and commercial evidence:

### 7.1 Most Favorable Situations

Foam fractionation is most advantageous as a concentration step when:

1. **PFAS profile is dominated by long‑chain PFAA**  
   – Long‑chains show near‑complete removal in groundwater, NF concentrate, and leachate at bench, pilot and commercial scale [S01, S03, S09, S11, S13, S15, S16].

2. **Matrix foaming and ionic strength are supportive**  
   – High ionic strength leachate and NF concentrates exhibit robust foam formation and enhanced adsorption [S01-E07, S09, S11, S16-E07].

3. **A destructive or secure disposal route for foamate exists**  
   – Incineration capacity [S12, S13], EO [S06; S08], plasma [S01], or HALT [S14] is available or can be added.

4. **Treatment goals focus on bulk mass removal**  
   – E.g., reducing load to downstream GAC/IX or meeting intermediate discharge standards where short‑chains at tens–hundreds ng/L are acceptable.

5. **Integration with existing aeration is feasible**  
   – FF can be bolted onto aeration steps in wastewater or leachate systems with added foam collection [S01-E01, S07, S11].

6. **Life‑cycle impacts of foam waste can be controlled**  
   – Using low foam fractions and/or multistage designs to minimize hazardous waste volume and incineration burden [S12, S14].

### 7.2 Less Favorable Situations

FF is less suitable as the primary concentration strategy when:

- **Short‑chain PFAS dominate the risk profile** and very low discharge limits must be achieved; even with co‑surfactants and advanced FF, short‑chains are only partially removed [S01, S03, S10, S11, S15, S16].
- **Matrix has low foaming potential** (e.g., biologically treated wastewater) and surfactant addition is undesirable because of residual surfactant toxicity and foaming downstream [S07, S10].
- **Sludge or high solids are present**, as FF co‑concentrates solids and PFAS, complicating foamate handling and potentially requiring dewatering steps [S07].
- **Robust destruction is not available** and the only feasible endpoint is long‑distance incineration of large foam volumes; here, high foam fractions (e.g., 20%) can generate burdensome waste volumes and life‑cycle impacts [S12, S13].

---

## 8. Evidence Gaps and Specific Research Needs

Key gaps and needs emerging from this evidence set include:

1. **Quantitative energy use and operational stability for full‑scale FF**  
   - Most operational energy data are modelled or qualitative [S12; S14; S16-E05]. Long‑term pilot/commercial campaigns with measured kWh/m³ and maintenance history are needed, particularly for leachate and municipal wastewater.

2. **Short‑chain PFAS control at environmentally relevant concentrations**  
   - While co‑surfactants and hybrid MER systems improve short‑chain removal in some settings [S05, S07, S09, S10], robust performance at ng/L levels in complex matrices remains uncertain. Comparative studies of co‑surfactant types vs ozone vs low‑pH operation on real waters would be valuable.

3. **Foamate speciation & byproducts across downstream technologies**  
   - EO data show persistent sulfonates in treated foam [S08]. HALT achieves high defluorination but leaves non‑mineralized organics [S14]. Systematic PFAS and co‑contaminant speciation (including precursors) through FF+EO, FF+HALT, and FF+plasma trains is needed.

4. **Aerosol emissions and air‑phase PFAS**  
   - Pilot FF and NF–FF studies document aerosols and PFOS in aerosol traps [S01, S09]. Field‑scale controls and emission measurements are necessary to ensure FF does not simply shift PFAS from water to air.

5. **Integrated treatment‑train optimization**  
   - Practical demonstration of multistage FF + HALT with internal recirculation [S14] and NF+FF+AIX configurations [S09] is pending. Detailed techno‑economic and environmental optimization (foam fraction vs short‑chain capture vs incineration burden) is particularly important, as highlighted by the LCA work [S12].

6. **Regulatory alignment for residuals**  
   - Several field and pilot studies reach long‑chain concentration targets while exceeding stringent multi‑PFAS sum criteria due to residual short‑chains [S15, S16]. Policy‑driven definitions of acceptable residual PFAS classes and concentrations will shape how FF‑based trains are designed.

---

## 9. Conclusions

The compiled evidence supports foam fractionation as a **mature, scalable separation technology** that:

- Efficiently removes and concentrates **long‑chain PFAS**,  
- Provides substantial **volume reduction and enrichment** of PFAS‑rich streams, enabling more feasible downstream destruction, and  
- Can be integrated with NF, EO, HALT, plasma or incineration as part of a **Separation + Concentration + Destruction** treatment train [S08; S09; S12; S13; S14].

However, FF:

- **Does not destroy PFAS**,  
- Often leaves **short‑chain PFAS and precursors** at levels incompatible with the lowest health‑based criteria, and  
- Produces foamate that is **co‑contaminated with organics and sometimes solids**, requiring deliberate, often energy‑intensive downstream management.

FF is thus best viewed as a **front‑end concentrator**—highly useful when appropriately coupled to robust destruction or polishing steps and when designed to minimize foam waste volumes and life‑cycle impacts.

        "text": "A removal method that could be highly suitable as a \ufb01rst step in such a treatment train process is foam fractionation, which exploits the surfactant properties of common PFAS and has been applied successfully in full scale for the remediation of PFAS-contaminated groundwater. 32\u221234 In foam fractionation, PFAS are adsorbed on the surface of gas bubbles rising through water. At the air \u2212water interface, these bubbles form a foam that is enriched in PFAS, so separation and collapse of the foam results in a concentrated foamate and a relatively PFAS- free retentate. 35 The process can be carried out in both batch and continuous operation. In continuous operation, stripping mode refers to operation with the liquid feed stream located above the liquid surface, whereas the feed enters below the foam/water interface in enriching mode. 35,36 Foam fractionation is a suitable water treatment technology for dilute solutions using only air, thereby eliminating the need for chemicals, solvents, \ufb01lter material, and adsorbents. 37 Leachate water is a particularly complex matrix to treat, requiring extensive pretreatment before conventional PFAS treatment, such as GAC, ion exchange, or membrane \ufb01ltration, can be applied successfully. 29 These matrix e \ufb00ects are less problematic in the case of foam fractionation due to a bene\ufb01cial e \ufb00ect of high ionic strength on the process"

claim_assessments.claim_text: PFAS are transferred from bulk water into a PFAS‑rich foam or foamate, often with substantial enrichment and volume reduction, while treated water retains reduced but non‑zero PFAS levels [S01; S07; S09; S11; S13; S15; S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: All cited studies describe foam fractionation as transferring PFAS from bulk water/leachate into foam/foamate, with reduced but non-zero PFAS remaining in treated water: S01 (landfill leachate, ~60% ΣPFAS removal, foamate ~10% volume), S07 (municipal wastewater; PFAS removed to foamate, FFout still contains PFAS), S09 (NF concentrate FF; permeate cleaned, retentate and foamate streams with PFAS), S11 (landfill leachate; PFAS concentrated in foamate up to 800 µg/L, bulk residuals), S13 & S15 (SAFF groundwater/leachate where treated water still has ng/L PFAS, and foamate is enriched), S16 (effluent and leachate cases with enriched foam and residual PFAS in bottom solution). All support phase transfer with enrichment and non-zero residuals.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Multiple studies explicitly position foam fractionation as the first step in a treatment train that must be followed by destruction or polishing adsorption processes [S01; S07; S08; S09; S11; S12; S13; S14; S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E01 & E05 describe FF as a suitable first step in a treatment train and propose downstream degradative treatment of concentrated foam by plasma or EO. S07-E06 & E08 note FF foamate should undergo further fractionation and final destruction and mention integration with other WWTP processes. S08-E01 & E04 frame FF explicitly as a preconcentration step before EO. S09-E07 & E08 propose downstream destruction (EO, incineration) for foamate and AIX polishing for FF retentate. S11-E04 mentions ozone FF followed by destruction technologies (plasma, thermal, EO). S12-E02–E04 model FF plus incineration and discuss FF as separation front-end, comparing to GAC/IX and hybrid trains. S13-E03 discusses SAFF as separation+concentration followed by incineration or development of destruction cells. S14-E01 & E04 explicitly focus on coupling FF with HALT as a concentration–destruction train. S16-E02, E04, E06 emphasize FF as a separation step that leaves residual PFAS and produces a concentrated foam suitable for disposal or further treatment. Collectively they position FF as an initial concentration step, not a stand‑alone solution.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In synthetic groundwater without co‑surfactant, long‑chain PFOS and PFOA achieved plateau removals of ~90% and ~60%, respectively, at ~40 µg/L [S10].
claim_assessments.rationale: S10-E06 describes a control experiment in synthetic groundwater with no co‑surfactant where initial concentrations of PFOS, PFOA, PFBS, PFBA were ~40 µg/L and states that long‑chain PFOS and PFOA exhibited rapid removal, plateauing at approximately 90% and 60% respectively. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Short‑chain PFBS and PFBA performed worse than PFOS and PFOA in the same synthetic groundwater control, consistent with lower surface activity [S10].
claim_assessments.rationale: S10-E06 states PFOS and PFOA plateau at ~90% and ~60% removal and that PFBS and PFBA were part of the experiment with no co-surfactant and lower surface excess; however the excerpt truncates after mentioning PFBS and PFBA, without explicitly giving their plateau removals. The record-level assessment notes that PFBS/PFBA had lower performance, but the provided chunk doesn’t quantify this. The qualitative statement that they ‘performed worse’ is consistent with lower surface activity but only implicitly supported here.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Adding CTAB as a cationic co‑surfactant in synthetic groundwater expanded performance across 0.4–400 µg/L and achieved near‑complete removal of PFOS and PFOA in ~5 min, while PFBS and PFBA required ~50 min at the highest concentration to reach high removals, with 99% removal reported for PFBS and PFBA at the highest concentration [S10].
claim_assessments.rationale: S10-E02 and E05 (co‑surfactant tests) state that each PFAS was tested individually over 400–400,000 ng/L and that PFOS and PFOA exhibited near-complete removal in as short as 5 minutes. They also state that for PFBS and PFBA at the highest initial concentration (400,000 ng/L), 99% removal was achieved and that ‘the same level of removal was achieved for PFBS and PFBA after approximately 50 minutes of operation.’ However, the explicit link between the 99% value and the ‘~50 minutes’ time is partly inferred across sentences. The concentration range (0.4–400 µg/L) and near‑complete long‑chain removal in ~5 min are supported; the precise co‑occurrence of 99% and 50 min for the short‑chains is only indirectly stated, so the claim is slightly more specific than the excerpt.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In real Australian groundwater with SDS as co‑foaming agent, bench‑scale foam fractionation reduced PFHxS, PFOA and PFOS to below 0.1 ppb (detection limit) within 60 min, whereas PFBA was not effectively removed [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 states that foam fractionation with SDS removed PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS from Australian groundwater to below the analytical detection limit of 0.1 ppb within 60 min, but was unable to remove short-chain PFBA. This aligns with the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A pilot groundwater foam fractionation + EO train achieved ~60% mean ΣPFAS removal in the FF step, with ~90% removal of long‑chain PFAA and weaker removal of short‑chain PFAS [S08].
claim_assessments.rationale: S08-E06 reports that mean ΣPFAS removal effectiveness for FF was 60% in groundwater, and that long-chain PFAA removals reached approximately 90% in both groundwater and leachate, with better removal of long‑chains than short‑chains due to higher adsorption coefficients. This supports the numerical values and qualitative contrast.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A commercial SAFF deployment on PFAS‑contaminated groundwater at AACO previously achieved ≥99.8% removal of PFOS and PFOA and ≥98.4% of PFHxS, with post‑SAFF concentrations ≤12, ≤1 and ≤17 ng/L, respectively [S13-E06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S13-E06 states that SAFF at AACO removed ≥99.8% PFOS and PFOA and ≥98.4% PFHxS, with post‑SAFF concentrations of ≤12 ng/L (PFOS), ≤1.0 ng/L (PFOA), and ≤17 ng/L (PFHxS). This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A pilot nanofiltration plant treating AFFF‑impacted municipal groundwater reduced total detectable PFAS in permeate from ~77 ng/L to 1.4 ng/L and ΣPFAS4 from 56 ng/L to 1.0 ng/L [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E01 reports that NF reduced total detectable PFAS from approximately 77 ng/L to 1.4 ± 0.4 ng/L, and ΣPFAS4 from 56 ng/L to 1.0 ± 0.2 ng/L. This is exactly the claimed result.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Continuous pilot foam fractionation of the NF concentrate removed ~90±1% of total PFAS using air alone and 94% with a cationic co‑surfactant [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E01 and E05 state that continuous FF of concentrate using air alone removed approximately 90 ± 1% of PFAS, and with cationic co-surfactant removal increased to 94%. This directly supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The combined NF+FF train shifted PFAS into a foamate stream (~2% of NF feed volume) at >3000 ng/L (41× feed concentration), and an FF retentate (~18% of NF feed volume) enriched in short‑chain PFAS at 35 ng/L without co‑surfactant and 21 ng/L with co‑surfactant [S09].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E05 and E07 report that foamate composed ~2% of NF feed volume and contained >3000 ng/L PFAS, 41× NF feed concentration, and that the FF retentate was ~18% of feed volume with 35 ng/L PFAS, decreasing to 21 ng/L with co-surfactant and enriched in short‑chains (PFBA, PFBS, PFPeA, PFHxA). This matches all parts of the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A pilot continuous foam fractionation column treating real landfill leachate achieved ~60% plateau ΣPFAS removal, with >90% removal for individual long‑chain PFAS and <30% removal for certain short‑chain PFAS, and foamate volume ~10% of inlet volume [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E03 states ΣPFAS removal plateaued around 60% and that long‑chain PFAS had removal >90% while certain short‑chains were <30%. S01-E05 reports collected foamate volume ~10% of inlet. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Bench‑scale foam fractionation with co‑surfactants in landfill leachate achieved 1.2–4 log reductions for long‑chain PFAS and 1–2 logs for some short‑chain compounds when cationic/zwitterionic cosurfactants were used [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E05 and E07 indicate that all cosurfactants were effective for long‑chain PFAS, giving 1.2–4 log reductions, and that cationic and zwitterionic cosurfactants recovered 1–2 logs of some short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBS, PFPeS). This matches the statement.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A low‑pH (~2) membrane electrochemical reactor treating landfill leachate achieved 95.6% total PFAS removal, with 98.3% removal of PFSAs and 85.5% of PFCAs; short‑chain PFSAs (C≤6) reached 92.5–99.1% removal and short‑chain PFCAs (C≤6) 80.8–90% [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E06 and E02 state that the MER achieved 95.6% total PFAS removal, with 98.3% PFSAs and 85.5% PFCAs, and that short‑chain PFSAs (C≤6) were removed 92.5–99.1% and short‑chain PFCAs 80.8–90%. This supports the detailed percentages and conditions.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Volume of defoamed leachate after MER was only 24% of the initial volume, with the remainder entrained in foam and solids [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E04 reports that defoamed leachate volume after MER treatment was 24% of the initial volume and attributes the reduction to leachate entrainment in rising foam. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Acidification of landfill leachate to pH 2.0 without electrochemistry separated 83.1% of total PFAS into foam and 11.3% into precipitated solids; with 0.1 M NaHCO₃ pre‑addition, foam‑phase separation increased to 92.5% [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E02 and E03 state that simple pH adjustment to 2.0 resulted in 83.1% of PFAS in foam and 11.3% in settled solids, and that adding 0.1 M NaHCO₃ before pH adjustment increased PFAS separation in foam to 92.5%. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Batch foam fractionation on several MBR/MBBR/CAS effluents achieved average removals of 96±1% for ΣPFAS4, 93±1% for ΣPFOAeq, and 53±2% for ΣPFAS21 [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E08 reports average removals of 96±1% for ΣPFAS4, 93±1% for ΣPFOAeq, and 53±2% for ΣPFAS21 for municipal wastewater by foam fractionation. This directly supports the numbers.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Biologically treated municipal effluents had low foaming potential; foam (top water layer) was removed by suction rather than as a stable overflowing foam [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E08 states that biologically treated wastewater has low foaming potential and that separation was performed without adding surfactant by removing the top layer of water using suction. This matches the description.

claim_assessments.claim_text: An 8% foamate extraction fraction of treated liquid volume was used in the municipal wastewater experiments, and authors judged it difficult to reduce this below ~5% without loss of performance [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E05 notes that an 8% foamate extraction fraction was applied and that based on previous studies it is unlikely this fraction can be decreased below 5% while maintaining similar removal efficiency. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Adding cationic surfactant K15(+) in MBR effluents increased PFHpA removal from 48% to >76% (MBRsed), PFPeA from 16% to 44% (MBRout), and PFHxA from 29% to >89% (MBRout; statistically significant) [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E03 reports that with K15(+), PFHpA removal in MBRsed increased from 48% to >76%, PFPeA in MBRout from 16% to 44%, and PFHxA in MBRout from 29% to >89%, with only the PFHxA increase statistically significant (p = 0.01). This aligns with the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A multi‑stage foam fractionation with added thickener (HPMC) treated WWTP effluent with initial PFOS and PFOA of 34.8 and 8.6 ng/L, respectively, and reduced both to <5 ng/L, corresponding to 99% and 94% removal; PFOS and PFOA were enriched 19× and 17× in third‑stage foam, with PFAS mass recovery for most compounds (except PFBA) 70–130% [S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S16-E01 reports initial PFOS 34.8 ng/L and PFOA 8.6 ng/L, final concentrations <5 ng/L, removals 99% (PFOS) and 94% (PFOA), enrichment factors of about 19× and 17× after 3rd stage, and mass recoveries of 70–130% for each PFAS except PFBA. HPMC use is mentioned in the record. This fully supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In landfill leachate, single‑stage foam fractionation left PFBA, PFOA and PFOS in the bottom solution at 10²–10³ ng/L after the first stage, despite high nominal removals, indicating that FF alone cannot achieve very low health advisory levels and must be paired with GAC/IX or other polishing [S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S16-E04 notes that after 1st‑stage FF, PFBA, PFOA and PFOS concentrations in the bottom solution remained at 10²–10³ ng/L, and concludes that FF cannot feasibly reach the very low EPA health advisory levels and requires polishing steps like GAC or IX. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Foam fractionation co‑concentrated ~80% of TOC into foam in landfill leachate, while PFAS were <0.01% of TOC, so organic co‑contaminants dominate foamate mass [S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S16-E06 reports average TOC recovery of 103.4% in single-stage FF, that ~80% of TOC ended up in foam solution, and that PFAS accounted for <0.01% of TOC in the landfill leachate. This supports the conclusion that non-PFAS organics dominate foamate mass.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Commercial SAFF on landfill leachate produced post‑SAFF leachate with SLV‑11 PFAS sum of 1260 ng/L, dominated by short‑chain PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeA, PFBA, while longer‑chains summed to only 14.4 ng/L [S15].
claim_assessments.rationale: S15-E03 states that the sum of mean concentrations of SLV‑11 PFAS in the treated streams is 1260 ng/L, caused by short-chain PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeA, PFBA being less amenable to adsorption, and that the sum of the other seven longer-chain SLV‑11 species is 14.4 ng/L. This directly supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Ozone foam fractionation on landfill leachate removed >90% long‑chain PFAS and 8–95% of named short‑chain PFAS; some very short‑chain species (<4 perfluorinated carbons) had recoveries <10% [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E01 and E03 report that ozone foam fractionation removed more than 90% long-chain PFAS, and that removal for short-chain PFAS (PFBS, PFHxA, 5:3 FTCA, PFHpA, PFHxS, 6:2 FTS) ranged from 8–95%, with recoveries below 10% for some short-chains with fewer than four perfluorinated carbons. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Ozone foam fractionation produced foamate volumes 2–4× lower than air foam fractionation and foamate wettability <4% vs 7–13% for air, while still concentrating PFAS up to 800 µg/L and increasing the number of detected PFAS (including several precursors) in foamate [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E01 notes ozone foam fractionation generates foamate volumes 2–4 times less than air FF. S11-E05 reports air foam wettability 7–13% and ozone foam wettability below 4%. S11-E06 states that concentrated foamate had total PFAS up to 800 µg/L and a significantly increased number of PFAS detected, including 6:2 FTCA, PFECHS, FOSA, 8:2 FTS, N‑MeFOSAA. All elements of the claim are supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Air foam fractionation in the same landfill leachate saw 10–30 percentage‑point gains in removal for short‑chains (PFHxA, PFPeS) and ~20 points for PFOA when increasing air flow from 0.5 to 1 L/min, but remained less effective for the very short‑chains [S11].
claim_assessments.rationale: S11-E03 states that increasing air flow from 0.5 to 1 L/min increased removal of short-chain PFHxA and PFPeS by 10–30%, and PFOA by about 20%, and that complete removal of short-chains was unlikely in the studied timeframe, especially for very short ones. This supports the described improvements and limitation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Batch foam fractionation on biologically treated municipal wastewater without or with limited surfactant addition is described as low‑foaming, requiring suction removal of a top water layer rather than an overflowing foam [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E08 notes that biologically treated wastewater had low foaming potential, and separation was done by removing the top layer of water using suction without added surfactant in that configuration. That matches the description of low‑foaming behavior and suction-based removal.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Foam fractionation applied directly to sludge liquors (MBRsludge, CASsludge) showed significantly lower PFAS removal than for corresponding treated effluents, and foamate from sludge matrices had higher total solids than bulk liquid, indicating co‑concentration of biomass/solids with PFAS [S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S07-E07 reports significantly lower PFAS removal for MBRsludge and CASsludge compared with MBRout and CASout. S07-E02 states that in all sludge experiments, formed foamate had higher TS content than the bulk liquor, visually apparent and confirmed by TS. While PFAS co-concentration with solids is logically implied by foam fractionation, the excerpt does not explicitly state PFAS enrichment in the solids-laden foamate; that part is interpretive. Thus lower PFAS removal and higher solids in foamate are supported; explicit PFAS co-concentration with biomass is inferred.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Across matrices and scales, short‑chain PFAS removal is consistently weaker than that for long‑chain PFAS in simple air‑only foam fractionation [S01; S03; S07; S08; S09; S11; S12; S15; S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: Multiple sources report systematically lower removal for short-chain PFAS: S01-E03 (certain short-chains <30% vs >90% long-chains), S03-E02/E06 (PFBA poorly removed while PFHxS, PFOA, PFOS removed well), S07-E07 (long-chains have higher affinity for foam and sludge than short-chains, with minimal PFDA removal), S08-E06 (FF more effective for long-chains), S09-E05/E07 (short-chain-enriched retentate after FF; co-surfactants needed to boost short-chain removal), S11-E03 (short-chains 8–95% vs long-chains >90%, with some ultra‑short <10% recovery), S12-E02/E05 (LCA text notes long-chain removal >90% and short-chain typically ≤50%), S15-E03/E06 (short-chains poorly removed by SAFF, dominating residuals), S16-E01/E02/E04 (short-chains show lower removal and high residuals). Collectively, they support the generalization that short‑chain removal is consistently weaker in air‑only FF.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Cationic co‑surfactants (CTAB, Montaline C40, K15(+)) markedly improved removal of short‑chain PFPeA, PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeS in synthetic and NF‑concentrate systems [S09, S10, S07].
claim_assessments.rationale: S09-E03 reports that cationic co-surfactant Montaline C40 improved PFAS removal in batch tests and increased short-chain removals: PFPeA +67 percentage points, PFHxA +59, PFBS +83, PFPeS +44. S10-E02/E05 show that CTAB-enhanced FF achieved 99% removal for PFBS and PFBA at the highest concentration and improved short‑chain removal kinetics compared to controls. S07-E03 shows K15(+) increased PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA removals substantially. These data support marked improvements for the specified short-chains.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In synthetic systems using OTCS with micro‑nano bubbles, PFOA and PFOS removals approached ~99% in synthetic water; in natural lake and reservoir waters PFOA/PFOS removals exceeded 80% [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E07/E05 report that the OTCS-MNBs system achieved removal efficiencies of 98.73% and 99.21% for PFOA and PFOS in synthetic water. The same abstract text states that in practical water experiments with four lakes/reservoirs, removal efficiencies for PFOA/PFOS exceeded 80%. This aligns with the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Foam fractionation energy demand is qualitatively characterized as low‑energy and low‑consumables compared to membrane and EO systems [S01-E01; S08-E04; S16-E05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E01 notes that FF is suitable for dilute solutions using only air, eliminating chemicals, solvents, filter materials and adsorbents, implying low consumables. S08-E04 states FF’s advantages over adsorption and membrane preconcentration include low use of consumables and robustness against complex matrices. S16-E05 describes FF as having relatively simple equipment, low operation cost and energy consumption, and no need for reagent addition. These collectively support the qualitative characterization.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For multi‑stage foam fractionation treating 1,000,000 m³ groundwater, total FF energy was modeled as ~0.8 kWh/m³ (800,000 kWh), with HALT adding only 2.5–6.7% more energy in the 2‑stage scenario and <0.03% in the 3‑stage scenario [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E07 states that both two- and three-stage FF processes are assumed to require ~0.8 kWh/m³, so 1,000,000 m³ needs ~800,000 kWh. The same excerpt gives HALT energy for the two-stage concentrate as 20,020–53,900 kWh (2.5–6.7% of FF energy) and for the three-stage case <220 kWh (<0.03% of FF energy). This precisely supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Life‑cycle assessment for landfill leachate foam fractionation reports GWP of 818 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ for a one‑stage 20% foam fraction system, 357 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ for one‑stage 1% foam fraction, and 402 kg CO₂‑eq per 1000 m³ for a three‑stage system [S12].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E06 states that global warming potential is 818 kg CO₂‑eq for the one-stage 20% foam fraction, 357 for one-stage 1% foam fraction, and 402 for the three-stage system, all per 1000 m³ treated leachate. This matches exactly.

claim_assessments.claim_text: One‑stage foam fractionation with 20% foam fraction produces 200 m³ foam waste per 1000 m³ leachate treated [S12].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E04 notes that the conventional one-stage FF system with 20% foam fraction has large hazardous foam waste volume, specified as 200 m³ per 1000 m³ treated. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the LCA scenarios, foam wastes are assumed to go to hazardous waste incineration as the base‑case end‑of‑life option [S12].
claim_assessments.rationale: S12-E03 describes that in the one-stage systems, extracted foam (1% or 20% of input volume) is sent to hazardous waste incineration as the disposal unit. S12-E03/E04 and the records consistently define hazardous waste incineration as the modeled end-of-life for foamate. Thus the claim is supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: At AACO, SAFF tertiary foamate is stored on‑site and the default disposal pathway is high‑temperature incineration, pending development of on‑site destruction cells [S13].
claim_assessments.rationale: S13-E01/E03 describe that tertiary foamate, highly enriched in PFAS with reduced volume, is stored on-site awaiting periodic disposal, and S13-E03 states that default disposal of the highly enriched PFAS waste is high‑temperature incineration, with preference for future on-site destruction cells under development. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the pilot FF+EO study, overall mean PFAS degradation across treatment trains was ~50%, with long‑chains degraded up to 86% and short‑chains up to 31% [S08].
claim_assessments.rationale: S08-E05 states that the mean total PFAS degradation over the designed treatment train reached 50%, with long- and short-chain PFAS degrading up to 86% and 31%, respectively. This exactly matches.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Stirred‑batch foam fractionation removed 80–90% of 14C‑PFOA from synthetic solutions in 30 min, and 90–100% of PFOA in foamate was mineralized to 14CO₂ during electrochemical oxidation [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E06 reports that foam fractionation can remove 80–90% of PFOA in 200 mL stirred-batch tests within 30 min and that 90–100% of PFOA in the concentrated foamate was oxidized via EO, converting -14COOH to 14CO₂. This supports both removal and mineralization statements.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In 3500 mL double‑tank tests, foam fractionation removed 90% of 14C‑PFOA from WWTP effluent but only 50% from drainage‑ditch water; PFOA half‑lives during EO of foamate were 8.7–15 min [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E06 states that in 3500 mL tank experiments, foam fractionation was 90% effective at removing 14C‑PFOA from WWTP effluent but only 50% for drainage ditch water, and S06-E02 gives EO half-lives ranging from 8.7–15 min. This supports the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Two foam concentrates from field demonstrations (FC1 primary foam and FC2 tertiary foam) with initial PFAS up to g/L levels were treated by HALT at 350 °C, 1 M NaOH, achieving >90% degradation and defluorination of all 62 identified PFAS within 90 min, with inorganic fluoride production consistent with essentially complete C–F bond cleavage [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E05 (abstract) states that HALT applied to two foam concentrates (field FF demos) achieved >90% degradation and defluorination within 90 min at 350 °C, 1 M NaOH for all 62 PFAS identified. S14-E03 notes fluoride measurements were consistent with complete defluorination. S14-E02 documents mg/L–g/L PFAS concentrations in FC1 and FC2. This supports the full statement.

claim_assessments.claim_text: After hypothetical 99% PFAS mass removal by HALT, residual PFAS concentrations in the small concentrate volume are expected to be mg/L–µg/L, still orders of magnitude above original groundwater; blending treated concentrate back into the large FF influent stream is proposed instead of direct discharge [S14].
claim_assessments.rationale: S14-E04 explains that even with 99% PFAS mass removal, concentrations in the small treated concentrate would remain at mg/L–µg/L, about three orders of magnitude higher than original groundwater, and proposes blending this small volume back into the much larger FF influent instead of discharge. This matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In landfill leachate, single‑stage foam fractionation transferred ~80% of TOC into foam while PFAS contributed <0.01% of TOC; PFAS precursors were concentrated in foamate, as indicated by TOP assay increases in PFCAs and PFOS after oxidative assay [S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S16-E06 states that ~80% of TOC ended up in foam solution, PFAS accounted for <0.01% of TOC, and that TOP assay after FF showed increased PFCAs (PFBA, PFPeA, PFHpA, PFOA) and PFOS in original, treated, and foam samples, consistent with precursor transformation during TOP. This supports the claim that precursors are concentrated in foamate and revealed by TOP.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Across landfill leachate and municipal wastewater, foam‑based concentration is robust for long‑chain PFAS, can be enhanced for some short‑chains with co‑surfactants, ozonation, or low‑pH operation, but still tends to leave residual short‑chain PFAS in treated water [S01; S02; S03; S05; S07; S09; S11; S15; S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01 (pilot leachate) shows >90% long-chain removal, poor short-chain removal. S02 (leachate with cosurfactants) shows 1.2–4 log long-chain, 1–2 log short-chain for some species. S03 groundwater experiments show PFBA (short-chain) not removed even with SDS. S05 (MER and pH 2 foaming) demonstrates high long-chain and improved, but not complete, short-chain capture, with residual short-chain PFCAs. S07 shows long-chain PFAS removal good in wastewater, short-chains only partially improved by K15(+), and low removal in sludge. S09 demonstrates robust long-chain removal and reliance on co-surfactant to boost short-chain capture, leaving short-chain‑rich retentate. S11 highlights >90% long-chain removal in leachate, short-chains 8–95% with incomplete removal. S15 shows SAFF leaves a residual load dominated by short-chains. S16 across matrices notes better removal for long-chains, short-chains consistently poorer and residuals at 10²–10³ ng/L in leachate. Collectively, this supports the summarized pattern.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Foam fractionation by itself does not destroy PFAS and often leaves short‑chain PFAS and precursors at levels incompatible with the lowest health‑based criteria; it produces foamate that is co‑contaminated with organics and sometimes solids, requiring downstream management [S01; S03; S05; S07; S08; S11; S13; S14; S16].
claim_assessments.rationale: Multiple studies explicitly state FF is a separation/concentration method, not a degradation one: S01-E01/E05, S08-E01/E04, S13-E08, S16-E05. S16-E04 notes that even after high removal, PFBA, PFOA, PFOS remain at 10²–10³ ng/L in leachate, above new EPA health advisories, and polishing is required. S15-E03 shows post‑SAFF leachate sum SLV‑11 =1260 ng/L, exceeding 90 ng/L criteria, dominated by short-chains. S16-E06 shows TOC ~80% in foam and PFAS <0.01% of TOC, evidencing organic co-contaminants. S07-E02 indicates sludge foams are high in TS (biomass/solids). S03 and S05 both show foam-based systems leaving short-chain PFAS residues. S14 treats foam concentrates by HALT because of high PFAS and DOM content. Thus all pieces of the summary are well supported.
